t: True Revival Is Returning to God
v: Israel, return to Yahweh your God; for you have fallen because of your sin.
Take words with you, and return to Yahweh. Tell him, “Take away all iniquity, and accept that which is good. So we offer our lips as sacrifices of bulls.
Assyria can’t save us. We won’t ride on horses; neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, ‘Our gods!’ For in you the fatherless find mercy.”
“I will heal their waywardness. I will love them freely; for my anger is turned away from him.
I will be like the dew to Israel. He will blossom like the lily, and send down his roots like Lebanon.
His branches will spread, and his beauty will be like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon.
Those who dwell under his shadow will return. They will revive like the grain, and blossom like the vine. His type will be like the wine of Lebanon.
Ephraim will say, ‘What have I to do any more with idols?’ I answer, and will look after him. I am like a green fir tree; from me your fruit is found.”
Who is wise, that he may understand these things? Who is prudent, that he may know them? For the ways of Yahweh are right, and the righteous walk in them; but the rebellious stumble in them.
b: Through Hosea, God sends out a call to Israel: “Return to Yahweh.” The real problem is not only circumstances, but that people have left God. People fall not because God has abandoned them, but because they have strayed from his way. The beginning of revival is not outward excitement, but a heart that truly turns back.

God wanted his people to stop relying on Assyria and Egypt, and to stop trusting idols made by their hands. Today’s idols are not necessarily statues; they can be money, ability, reputation, relationships, and ourselves. When we build our security on the world, we easily drift from God; but true peace is found only in God.

Most precious is what God says: “I will heal their waywardness. I will love them freely.” God does not love us reluctantly; he loves us freely. Even if a person has fallen, as long as he is willing to turn back, God is still willing to restore, heal, and replant him. When a person is rooted in God again, he will blossom like the lily and bear fruit like the olive tree, and his life will once more be filled with fragrance and glory.
a: Truly turn back to God
Not just religious form, but genuine repentance.
Let go of the idols in your life
No longer rely on the world and on yourself.
Be rooted in God again
Let your life receive supply and fruit from the Lord.
q: Are there still idols in my life that take God’s place?
pr: Heavenly Father, draw my heart back to You again. Forgive me for relying on the world and on myself instead of depending on You with all my heart. Heal the straying and weakness within me, so that I may be rooted in You again and live a fragrant, fruitful life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will return to Yahweh and leave my idols; my life will be rooted again and bear fruit.

t: Those Who Truly Love God Will Stop to Love Others
v: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, and gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
b: This parable of the Good Samaritan shows us that true love is not only knowing the truth, but being willing to pay a price to love others. The priest and the Levite understood religion, yet they passed by on the other side; only the Samaritan, whom the Jews looked down on, stopped and showed mercy to the wounded man.

Many times it is not that people do not see the need, but that they are unwilling to stop. Love takes time, cost, and sacrifice. The Samaritan did not only sympathize; he personally bound up the wounds, set the man on his animal, took him to be cared for, and paid with his own money. True love is not just being moved; it is action.

Jesus ended by saying, “Go and do likewise.” God does not want us only to hear the Word, but to live it out. The 321 vision stresses “life before ministry”: a truly godly life will surely overflow with compassion. When people care only about their own affairs, they easily grow cold; but when Jesus lives within, we begin to see people’s needs.
a: Stop and care for people
Don’t be so busy that you lose compassion.
Live out love in action
Love is not only a feeling, but paying a price.
Become one who brings healing
Let others experience Christ’s love through you.
q: Who has been hurt, lonely, or in need of help lately whom I chose to ignore?
pr: Heavenly Father, give me a heart of compassion, and do not let me stay only in religion and knowledge. Help me, like the Good Samaritan, to stop when I see a need and to pay the price to love. May Jesus’ love flow out from my life and become comfort and help to others. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will live out Christ’s compassion and serve people with love and action.

t: Let Christ Have First Place in Everything
v: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him.
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.
He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.
For it was the Father’s good pleasure that in him all the fullness should dwell;
and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.
You, being in time past alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil works,
yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without blemish and blameless before him,

if it is so that you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast, and not moved away from the hope of the Good News which you heard, which was proclaimed in all creation under heaven; of which I, Paul, was made a servant.
b: This passage lets us see who Jesus truly is: he is not only a great teacher, but the Creator of all things. Heaven and earth and everything in them were made through him and for him. The greatest problem in human life is that people have left the Creator and begun to center on themselves; but the true order of life is to let Christ have first place.

The passage says, “In him all things are held together.” Today people think they can control their lives, but the one who truly holds our lives together is Christ. Without him, a person is ultimately empty, confused, and without direction. Only when we let Jesus be King does life realign with its true center.

Most precious of all, through the cross Jesus has reconciled us to God. People who were separated from God by sin can now return to the Father. This is not by human effort, but by the blood Christ shed. He not only forgives our sins; he will bring us into holiness, steadfastness, and eternal hope.
a: Let Jesus have first place
Not only confess him with your mouth, but let the Lord rule in your daily life.
Be rooted in the Good News
Do not be shaken by the world’s values.
Live in the grace of being reconciled to God
No longer live in condemnation and separation.
q: Who or what is the true center of my life: Jesus, or myself?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for reconciling me to Yourself through Jesus. Help me no longer to center on myself, but to let Christ have first place in my life. Make me grounded and steadfast in the true faith, not moved by the world, and living every day in the hope of the Good News. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Jesus is the center of my life; I will let Christ have first place in everything.

t: God’s Word Is the Wisdom of Life
v: how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day.
Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies, for they are always with me.
I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation.
I understand more than the aged, because I have kept your precepts.
I have restrained my feet from every evil way, that I might observe your word.
I have not turned aside from your ordinances, for you have taught me.
How sweet are your promises to my taste, more than honey to my mouth!
Through your precepts, I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way.
b: The psalmist did not read God’s Word reluctantly; he “loved” God’s law. He discovered that God’s Word is not only knowledge, but the way of life. The world has many voices, concepts, and methods, but the only thing that can truly lead a person toward life is God’s truth.

The passage says, “Your commandments make me wiser than my enemies, for they are always with me.” True wisdom is not just a clever mind, but knowing how to live within God’s will. Many people have great knowledge, yet their lives are still in confusion; but a person who reveres God and does his Word lives with true stability and discernment.

The psalmist also says, “How sweet are your promises, more than honey.” When a person truly experiences God’s Word, he no longer treats Bible reading as a duty, but discovers that God’s Word can comfort, enlighten, renew, and heal the heart. God’s Word is not a cold set of rules, but the supply of heavenly life.
a: Meditate on God’s Word every day
Let truth be the direction of your life.
Discern your path by God’s Word
Reject the world’s wrong values.
Live out obedience
Not only hear the Word, but actually do it.
q: Toward God’s Word, do I feel duty, or a true love for it?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for giving us Your precious Word. Let me not only know the Bible, but truly love Your truth. Shine on me and guide me with Your Word, so that I stay far from evil ways and live in Your wisdom and life. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I love God’s Word; God’s truth will become the wisdom and the path of my life.

t: Jesus Offered Himself Once and Completed Salvation
v: For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually every year, make perfect those who draw near.
Otherwise, wouldn’t they have ceased to be offered, because the worshippers, having been once cleansed, would have had no more consciousness of sins?
But in those sacrifices there is a yearly reminder of sins.
For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins.
Therefore when he comes into the world, he says, “Sacrifice and offering you didn’t desire, but you prepared a body for me;
in whole burnt offering and sacrifices for sin you had no pleasure.
Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do your will, God.’”
Previously saying, “Sacrifices and offerings, whole burnt offerings, and sacrifices for sin you didn’t desire, neither had pleasure in them” (those which are offered according to the law),
then he has said, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He takes away the first, that he may establish the second,
by which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
b: In the Old Testament, people had to offer sacrifices again and again, because those sacrifices could only cover sin for a time and could not truly remove it. The blood of bulls and goats could not change a person’s life, nor fully cleanse the conscience. So every year people had to offer sacrifices again, and were reminded of their sins once more.

But Jesus came. He did not bring another sacrifice; he offered himself. The cross is not a repeated religious ritual, but a once-for-all, eternal salvation. Jesus took our judgment in his own body, so that we can truly be reconciled with God.

The passage specifically says, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” Jesus’ greatest victory was not only suffering, but perfect obedience to God the Father. Satan fell through rebellion; Jesus was glorified through obedience. Today we too are not saved by religious works, but by the grace Christ has already completed. True faith is not people striving to earn God’s acceptance, but receiving by faith the salvation Jesus has already accomplished.
a: Stop trying to be justified by works
Trust in Jesus’ cross alone.
Live in cleansing and grace
Do not stay in condemnation.
Learn to obey God’s will
Follow Jesus’ heart of obedience to the Father.
q: Am I still trying to earn God’s acceptance by my own effort?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus to be the perfect sacrifice. Thank You that I am not saved by my own effort, but forgiven and cleansed through Christ. Help me to live in grace, and to learn, like Jesus, to obey Your will. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Jesus has completed salvation once for all; through Christ I am cleansed, justified, and set free.

t: Do Not Exalt People; Exalt God Alone
v: Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ.
I fed you with milk, not with meat; for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, you aren’t even now ready,
for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the way of men?
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?
Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed; and each as the Lord gave to him?
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
So then neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
Now he who plants and he who waters are one, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
b: Paul pointed out a great problem in the Corinthian church: although they believed in the Lord, they were still living in the flesh. How could this be seen? They were jealous of one another, quarreled, and exalted people. Some said they belonged to Paul, others to Apollos. When people begin to exalt people, comparison, division, and factions easily arise.

The truly spiritual person does not put his focus on people but on God. Paul said very clearly, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” People are only vessels; the one who truly changes lives is God. If glory is given to people, we easily lose our reverence for God.

Today the church and ministry easily fall into the same problem: exalting speakers, exalting gifts, exalting teams, while forgetting that the real protagonist is Jesus. The 321 vision reminds us: the focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on people, not on circumstances. A truly mature life becomes more and more humble, and knows more and more that everything is God’s grace.
a: Do not exalt people
Respect the vessel, but give glory to God alone.
Stay away from jealousy and strife
Do not live in comparison and factions.
Be faithful in your own role
Whether planting or watering, do it for the Lord.
q: Is my focus now more on Jesus, or on people?
pr: Heavenly Father, forgive me for sometimes exalting people, comparing myself with others, and even quarreling over people. Let me fix my eyes on Jesus again, knowing that all growth in life is Your work. Help me also to be faithful in the role You have entrusted to me, and not to take Your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I do not exalt people; I exalt Jesus alone. It is God alone who makes life grow.

t: The Love of the Cross Establishes an Eternal New Covenant
v: When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles.
He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.
For I tell you, I will not eat of it any more until it is fulfilled in the Kingdom of God.”
He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this, and share it among yourselves,
for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until the Kingdom of God comes.”
He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and gave to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.”
Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.”
“But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table.
For the Son of Man indeed goes, as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!”
They began to question among themselves which of them it was who would do this thing.
b: Just before going to the cross, the one thing Jesus most wanted to do was to eat this last supper with his disciples. He knew he was about to suffer, be betrayed, and be crucified, yet he still said, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you.” This was not merely a meal; it was a farewell full of love and grace.

When Jesus took the bread and said, “This is my body which is given for you,” and took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood,” he declared that salvation was about to be completed. From then on, people no longer need to earn God’s acceptance by their own effort; through Jesus’ sacrifice they can be reconciled with God. The cross is not the end of love, but love’s deepest expression.

Most moving of all, Jesus knew that Judas would betray him, yet he still let him sit at the table. This shows us that God’s love is not built on whether a person deserves it, but on God’s unchanging grace. When we were still weak, failing, and in debt, the Lord had already loved us first.

The cross also shows us the way of true life. The world seeks to exalt itself, but Jesus chose to give himself up; the world seeks its own interest, but Jesus willingly gave for others. When Christ lives in us, we too learn to stop centering on ourselves and let love become the motive of our lives, willing to care for others, serve others, and help others succeed, so that the Lord’s life flows out through us.
a: Remember the Lord’s grace often
Do not let the cross become a familiar story that no longer moves you.
Live in God’s love
Believe that you are accepted, and no longer live in condemnation and accusation.
Respond to the Lord’s love with love
Learn to give yourself up, care, and serve those around you.
q: Am I still moved by the love of the cross, and willing to respond to the Lord’s love with my life?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus to give his life for me. Thank You that the Lord, with his own body and precious blood, established an eternal new covenant for me. Help me to remember the grace of the cross always, not only knowing Your love but truly living in Your love. Help me follow Jesus in giving myself up, and let Your love flow through me to more people. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will remember the love of the cross and live out the life of Christ.

t: Walking Together Is Stronger Than Walking Alone
v: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one be warm alone?
If someone prevails against him who is alone, two will withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
b: God never created people to live alone. From Genesis, God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” Life is a journey, not a lone battle. Many think that relying on themselves is the most reliable, but God has placed loving and supporting one another within his plan.

Solomon said, “Two are better than one.” When one falls, the other can lift him up. In life we inevitably meet weakness, failure, discouragement, and setbacks. Sometimes a word of encouragement, a prayer, or a companion’s presence can help a person stand again. God often brings his love and strength into our lives through those around us.

Not only that, spiritual growth also needs companions. Walking alone, it is easy to lose our way; with people reminding and encouraging one another, we can move forward together toward God’s will. True relationships are not about using one another but about helping one another succeed; not comparing, but supporting one another.

The passage ends, “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” When two people walk together in unity, with God in the midst, the relationship becomes even stronger. Whether husband and wife, family, friends, co-workers, or members of the church, when everyone puts God at the center, we can build solid relationships of life in love.
a: Treasure those God has given to walk with you
Give thanks for those who accompany you in life.
Take the initiative to support the weak
Do not only receive help, but become help to others.
Build God-centered relationships
Let God be the foundation of every relationship.
q: In my life, do I have companions who are willing to support one another and pursue God together?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for not asking me to walk alone. Thank You for accompanying my life’s journey through family, friends, and brothers and sisters. Help me treasure these relationships, and let me be a blessing and support to others. May we follow You together, build one another up in love, and grow together in truth. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will walk with God, and walk with those who love the Lord.

t: Those Who Wait for Yahweh Will Renew Their Strength
v: “To whom then will you liken me, that I should be equal?” says the Holy One.

Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name. By the greatness of his might, and because he is strong in power, not one is lacking.
Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel, “My way is hidden from Yahweh, and the justice due me is disregarded by my God?”
Haven’t you known? Haven’t you heard? The everlasting God, Yahweh, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary. His understanding is unsearchable.
He gives power to the weary. He increases the strength of him who has no might.
Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall;
but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.
b: This passage is God’s comfort to the weary. At that time Israel was in distress and thought God had forgotten them, so they complained, “My way is hidden from Yahweh.” But God answered them: the Lord who created the universe has never forgotten you, and has never stopped working.

God first lifts people’s eyes from their problems to the Creator. “Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these.” When we keep looking at circumstances, we easily lose heart; when we fix our eyes on God, faith is restored. The God who counts the stars and calls them by name also knows your name, your tears, and your situation.

The passage does not say that believers never grow weary; instead it admits, “Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall.” Even the strongest and most capable have limits. But God’s power has no limit. When a person admits his lack and turns to wait on God, God gives heavenly strength.

Waiting for Yahweh is not passive waiting, but looking to God in faith, depending on him, and obeying him. An eagle soars not by frantically flapping its wings, but by making use of the rising air currents. In the same way, those who belong to God do not struggle on in their own strength but learn to rely on God’s power. When we are willing to lay down our own methods and quietly seek God’s guidance, we can experience renewal and strength from God.
a: Turn your eyes from the problem to God
Don’t keep looking at circumstances; look up to the Lord who created heaven and earth.
Admit your limits
Don’t struggle on by yourself, but depend on God.
Practice waiting on God
Renew your strength through prayer, Bible reading, and quiet time near the Lord.
q: Lately, have I been running in my own strength, or waiting on Yahweh and drawing on his power?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for not leaving me when I am weary and weak. Help me not to look only at circumstances, but to fix my eyes on You. Give me new strength, new hope, and new faith, so that I may mount up with wings like eagles. Whatever the road ahead, I am willing to wait on You, trust You, and follow You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will fix my eyes on God, and in the Lord I will renew my strength.

t: Jesus Is the Good Shepherd Who Seeks the Lost Sheep
v: The word of Yahweh came to me, saying,

“Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy, and tell them, even the shepherds, ‘The Lord Yahweh says: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep?
“‘For the Lord Yahweh says: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.

As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so I will seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.

I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the watercourses, and in all the inhabited places of the country.

I will feed them with good pasture, and their fold will be on the mountains of the height of Israel. There they will lie down in a good fold. They will feed on rich pasture on the mountains of Israel.
I will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down,’ says the Lord Yahweh.

‘I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick; but the fat and the strong I will destroy. I will feed them in justice.’”
b: Through the prophet Ezekiel, God rebuked the shepherds of that time, because they cared only for themselves and not for the flock. God had entrusted them to care for his people, but they pursued their own interests and neglected the needs of the sheep. So God declared, “I myself, even I, will search for my sheep.”

This is one of the warmest promises in the whole Bible. When people are lost, God does not give up; when people fall, God does not leave; when people are wounded, God does not scold. He comes himself to seek, rescue, heal, and restore. This promise is fully fulfilled in Jesus. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11)

God specifically mentions four kinds of sheep: the lost, the driven away, the broken, and the sick. These are also the real conditions of many people’s lives. Some have lost their way, some are driven to a dead end by circumstances, some are wounded in spirit, and some have lived in weakness for a long time. But God despises none of these sheep. He seeks the lost, brings back those who have strayed, heals the wounded, and strengthens the weak.

Today we are not only those who are shepherded; we are also called to be a blessing to others. When we experience the Lord’s love, we can bring this love to those around us. As God has accepted us, we learn to accept others; as God has supported us, we learn to support others. This is the overflow of Christ’s life.
a: Believe that God is seeking you
Even when you are lost or weak, do not doubt God’s love.
Bring your wounds to the Lord
Let Jesus heal your life.
Become one who cares for others
Share the love you have received from God.
q: In what areas of my life do I need the Good Shepherd to seek, heal, and restore me?
pr: Heavenly Father, thank You for being my Good Shepherd. When I was lost, You sought me; when I was wounded, You healed me; when I was weak, You supported me. Help me experience Your love more deeply, and let me become a comfort and blessing to others, bringing Your love to those around me who are in need. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: Yahweh is my shepherd; I will follow him to the end.

t: Living as a Child of God
v: Behold, how great a love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God! Therefore the world doesn’t know us, because it didn’t know him.
Beloved, now we are children of God, and it is not yet revealed what we will be. But we know that, when he is revealed, we will be like him; for we will see him just as he is.
Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure.
By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart of compassion against him, how does the love of God remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, neither with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.
b: The apostle John first reminds us of a most precious fact: we are children of God. This identity is not earned by effort or won by performance. It comes from the Father’s great love. When we receive Jesus Christ, we are welcomed into God’s family and become his beloved children.

God does not only give us a new identity; he also shapes us into a new life. John says, “when he is revealed, we will be like him.” Faith is not merely waiting to enter eternity someday. It is being changed by the Lord today. As we draw near to him and obey him, our lives look more and more like Jesus.

Then John turns our attention to love. Jesus laid down his life for us, and so we learn what true love is. Love is not stuck in our feelings, nor is it only on our lips. It is willing to give, willing to sacrifice, willing to help others flourish. The cross is the truest expression of God’s love.

So God’s children do not only receive love; they live it out. If we see someone’s need and remain unmoved, it is hard to say that God’s love fills us. A truly God-centered life turns love into action, so that the people around us feel the warmth and grace of Christ through us.
a: Live in your identity as God’s child
Do not let the world’s standards define you. Believe that you are a child the Father loves.
Pursue becoming more like Jesus
Through prayer and Bible reading each day, let your life be renewed again and again.
Express love through action
Reach out to those in need and put love into practice in daily life.
q: Am I truly living out my identity as God’s child, and showing the love of Christ through my actions?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me with such great love and making me Your child. Help me live in this precious identity and no longer be swayed by the values of the world. Make me more and more like Jesus, and let me live out Your love in everyday life, caring for and blessing the people around me, not only in words but in deeds. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will live as a child of God and let the love of Christ flow out through my life.

t: A Heart of Reverence and Joy before God
v: David was afraid of Yahweh that day; and he said, “How can the ark of Yahweh come to me?”
So David was not willing to move the ark of Yahweh to be with him in the city of David, but David carried it aside into the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite.
The ark of Yahweh remained in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite three months; and Yahweh blessed Obed-Edom and all his house.

It was told King David, “Yahweh has blessed the house of Obed-Edom, and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God.” David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-Edom into the city of David with joy.
When those who bore the ark of Yahweh had gone six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf.
David danced before Yahweh with all his might; and David was clothed in a linen ephod.
So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of Yahweh with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet.
b: After his first attempt to bring up the ark failed, David’s heart was full of fear and confusion. He had been zealous, but he had not done things God’s way, and Uzzah was struck down. David learned that loving God takes more than passion; it also requires respecting God’s truth and his ways.

So the ark was sent to Obed-Edom’s house for three months. Surprisingly, God’s presence brought no disaster there, but rich blessing. God’s presence is the very source of blessing. When people draw near to God in the way he desires, his grace reaches their families, their work, and every part of their lives.

When David heard that Obed-Edom had been blessed, he went to bring the ark up again. This time he did not rely on his own methods but did as God had commanded. When we turn from our own way to God’s way, we can experience his presence and joy once more.

The passage especially describes David dancing before Yahweh with all his might. He was not performing for others or displaying his status; he simply rejoiced in God’s presence. True worship is not a religious ritual. It is a heart that reveres God, loves God, and delights in God.
a: Approach God in the right way
Zeal is not enough; we must also obey God’s truth.
Treasure God’s presence
God’s presence is the greatest blessing in life.
Make God your greatest joy
Do not seek only God’s gifts; seek the God who gives them.
q: Am I seeking God’s blessings, or am I seeking God himself?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being willing to dwell with people. Help me to have not only zeal but also an obedient heart that follows You according to Your truth. Help me treasure Your presence and make You my greatest satisfaction and joy. May my life be filled with reverence and thanksgiving as I live in Your grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will revere God and draw near to him, making his presence my greatest joy.

t: True Wisdom Sees the Heart
v: Then two women who were prostitutes came to the king, and stood before him.
The one woman said, “Oh, my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house; and I delivered a child with her in the house.
The third day after I delivered, this woman delivered also. We were together. There was no stranger with us in the house, only we two in the house.
This woman’s child died in the night, because she lay on it.
She arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me while your servant slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom.
When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, it was dead; but when I had looked at it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, whom I bore.”
The king said, “Get me a sword.” They brought a sword before the king.
The king said, “Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.”

Then the woman whose the living child was spoke to the king, for her heart yearned over her son, and she said, “Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and in no way kill it!” But the other said, “It shall be neither mine nor yours; divide it.”
Then the king answered, “Give her the living child, and in no way kill it. She is its mother.”
All Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do justice.
b: This is one of King Solomon’s most famous judgments. Two women each insisted on her own story, with no evidence and no witnesses. From a human point of view, it was almost impossible to tell who the real mother was. Yet the wisdom God gave Solomon was more than a sharp mind; it was the ability to see into the human heart.

When Solomon proposed dividing the child, the real mother was stricken to the core. She would rather lose her child than see him harmed. True love cares most not about its own rights but about the other’s life. Love is always willing to sacrifice itself for the good of another.

This passage also reminds us that God looks not only at people’s words but at their hearts. People can see only appearances and actions, but God searches the heart. Often we think we are right, while the real problem lies hidden deep within. Ask God for heavenly wisdom, so that we see more than the surface of things and understand his heart.

True wisdom is not about making ourselves look clever; it is about letting people see God’s glory. Solomon did not exalt himself, and the people’s awe was directed not at Solomon but at the God who gave him wisdom. When we humbly depend on God, he will guide us in the right path in our choices and judgments.
a: Seek wisdom that comes from God
For important decisions, do not rely on experience alone; seek God’s guidance.
Practice starting from love
In conflicts and disputes, learn to think of what is good for others.
Value the heart over appearances
Ask God to purify our motives and thoughts.
q: When I must judge a situation or a person, do I rely on my own cleverness, or do I seek God’s wisdom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being the source of wisdom. Give me heavenly wisdom, so that in every situation I do not rely on my own cleverness but understand Your heart. Give me also a heart full of love, willing to think of what is good for others. Let my life not exalt myself but bring glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will depend on God’s wisdom and live out his heart with love.

t: Love at the Last Supper before the Cross
v: Now when evening had come, he was reclining at the table with the twelve disciples.
As they were eating, he said, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.”
They were exceedingly sorrowful, and each one began to ask him, “It isn’t me, is it, Lord?”
He answered, “He who dipped his hand with me in the dish, the same will betray me.
The Son of Man goes, even as it is written of him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”
Judas, who betrayed him, answered, “It isn’t me, is it, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You said it.”
As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. He gave to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.”
He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave to them, saying, “All of you drink it,
for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.
But I tell you that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s Kingdom.”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
b: This was the last meal Jesus shared with his disciples before he was crucified. What is startling is that, even knowing he would soon be betrayed, humiliated, and nailed to a cross, Jesus was still concerned not for himself but for his disciples and the salvation of all humanity. Here we see that true love is not centered on self but is willing to give everything for others.

When Jesus said, “one of you will betray me,” the disciples did not suspect one another. Each one asked, “It isn’t me, is it, Lord?” This is an attitude worth learning. A spiritually mature person does not first inspect other people’s faults but examines his own heart. Often the greatest danger lies not in our circumstances but in whether we still come humbly before the Lord.

Then Jesus took the bread and the cup and established the Lord’s Supper. The bread represents his body, soon to be given up, and the cup his blood, shed for the world. By giving his own life, Jesus established the new covenant, so that all who believe in him can receive forgiveness and eternal life. The cross is not a tragedy; it is the center of God’s plan of salvation. It is not defeat; it is the greatest victory of love.

Finally, they sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives. Jesus knew that the agony of Gethsemane and the suffering of the cross lay ahead, yet he obeyed the Father’s will and kept walking forward. True faith is not the absence of difficulty; it is choosing to trust and follow God even in the midst of it.
a: Examine yourself often
Do not look only at others’ problems; first come before God and search your own heart.
Remember the Lord’s love often
Reflect on the grace of Jesus giving his body and shedding his blood for us.
Obey God’s leading
Even when difficulties lie ahead, trust that God’s will is always good.
q: Facing the love of the cross, do I stop at being moved, or do I respond to the Lord with my whole life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for sending Jesus Christ to give His body and shed His blood for my sins. Help me always to remember the grace of the cross, not only receiving Your love but also responding to it with my life. Give me a humble, teachable heart that examines itself often, and an obedient heart that is willing to follow You to the end, whatever the circumstances. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will remember the Lord’s love and follow Jesus faithfully all my life.

t: Each Doing Their Part, Building Up the Body of Christ Together
v: For I say, through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think soberly, as God has apportioned to each one a measure of faith.
For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
Having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us, whether prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
b: Paul reminds us not to think of ourselves more highly than we ought. Pride makes people overestimate themselves, and low self-esteem makes them underestimate themselves, but God wants us to know ourselves rightly according to the grace he has given. True humility is not thinking we are worthless; it is knowing that everything we have is a gift of God’s grace.

Paul then uses the body as a picture of the church. A body has eyes, ears, hands, and feet. Each part functions differently, yet each is equally important. If the eye envies the ear and the ear is jealous of the hand, the whole body cannot work in health. In the same way, in God’s household everyone has different gifts and roles, and no one is more important than another.

God never asked everyone to become the same kind of person. He asks each of us to be faithful to our own calling. Some are good at teaching, some at caring, some love to serve, and some are good at encouraging. When everyone is willing to use the gifts God has given, working together and building one another up, the body of Christ grows in health.

So we do not need to compare ourselves with others or envy their gifts. God has never made two leaves exactly alike, nor two people exactly alike. What matters is not whether I can become someone else, but whether I am faithfully becoming the person God wants me to be, and giving the glory to God.
a: Know yourself rightly
Be neither proud nor self-deprecating; see yourself through God’s eyes.
Discover and use your gifts
Find the role God has entrusted to you and serve faithfully.
Learn to work together
Appreciate others’ gifts and build up God’s household together.
q: Am I faithfully using the gifts God has given me to serve him and help others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for making me a unique person and giving me gifts and a calling. Help me not to compare myself with others, nor to look down on myself, but to serve faithfully according to Your heart. Teach me to appreciate others’ gifts and to work together with my brothers and sisters, building up Your church in unity, for the glory of Your holy name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will faithfully use the gifts God has given me and build up God’s household together with my brothers and sisters.

t: When You See God’s Presence, Fear Fades
v: The man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying, “Beware that you not pass such a place; for the Syrians are coming down there.”
The king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once or twice.
The heart of the king of Syria was very troubled about this thing; and he called his servants, and said to them, “Won’t you show me which of us is for the king of Israel?”
One of his servants said, “No, my lord, O king; but Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel the words that you speak in your bedroom.”
He said, “Go and see where he is, that I may send and get him.” It was told him, “Behold, he is in Dothan.”
Therefore he sent horses, chariots, and a great army there. They came by night, and surrounded the city.
When the servant of the man of God had risen early and gone out, behold, an army with horses and chariots was around the city. His servant said to him, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?”
He answered, “Don’t be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”

Elisha prayed, and said, “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
b: Elisha’s servant rose early and saw enemy troops surrounding the whole city, and he was immediately gripped by fear. In his eyes there was only danger, threat, and despair. This is how many of us react to trouble: when our eyes see only circumstances, fear easily takes control.

Elisha’s reaction was entirely different. He said, “Don’t be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Elisha did not deny the crisis; he saw the reality his servant could not see. He knew God’s presence was more real than the trouble before them, and God’s power greater than the enemy’s strength.

So Elisha prayed, “Yahweh, please open his eyes.” When God opened the servant’s eyes, he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire all around them. God’s protection had been there all along; he simply had not seen it. Often our problem is not that God is absent, but that we see only the problem and not God.

Life inevitably brings illness, pressure, challenges, and hardship. But faith is not about how big the circumstances are; it is about how big God is. When we fix our eyes on God, we find that he has already gone ahead to open the way and has been guarding us all along. When our eyes turn from the problem to God, fear is replaced by faith.
a: Don’t look only at circumstances
Difficulties are real, but God’s presence is more real.
Look to God in faith often
Learn to see things from God’s perspective, not only from a human one.
Pray for spiritual eyes to be opened
See that God is at work, and see his protection and guidance.
q: Facing my present difficulty, do I see the problem, or do I see the God who is with me?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when I face difficulties and challenges, do not let me see only the circumstances, but let me see Your presence and power. Open my eyes, so that I understand You have always been at my side, protecting and guiding me. Help me not to be bound by fear but to trust You in faith and walk in the path You have prepared. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will fix my eyes on God, for the One who is with me is greater than the world.

t: Strong in Grace, Faithful to the Gospel to the End
v: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
You therefore must endure hardship, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enlisted him as a soldier.
Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.
Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.
Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my Good News,
in which I suffer hardship to the point of bonds as a malefactor. But the word of God isn’t bound.
Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
This saying is faithful: for if we died with him, we will also live with him.
If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us.
If we are faithless, he remains faithful. He can’t deny himself.
b: Paul wrote these words near the end of his life. He was in prison, facing persecution and the threat of death, yet his greatest concern was not his own situation but that the gospel would be passed on. So he urged Timothy, “be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” True strength does not come from willpower; it is drawn from the grace of Christ.

Paul then gives three pictures of those who follow the Lord. A soldier gives himself wholly to his mission and is not entangled in the affairs of life; an athlete keeps the rules and runs hard; a farmer labors diligently and waits patiently for the harvest. The spiritual path calls for focus, faithfulness, and perseverance. Growth in life does not come overnight; it matures slowly through daily obedience.

Even bound in chains, Paul declared, “the word of God isn’t bound.” Circumstances can limit a person but cannot stop God’s work. Through the ages, many servants of God have suffered persecution and hardship, yet the gospel has kept spreading, because God reigns forever.

Finally, Paul brings the focus back to Jesus. We may be weak, we may fall, and at times our faith may be small, but God is always faithful. Human faith rises and falls; God’s faithfulness never changes. So we can safely place our lives in his hands and follow him faithfully to the end.
a: Draw strength from grace
Don’t rely on yourself alone; learn to depend on the Lord every day.
Give yourself to God’s commission
Don’t let worldly things steal your focus from God.
Hold fast to faith in hardship
Believe that God still reigns and his promises never fail.
q: Am I holding on by my own strength right now, or am I being strengthened in the grace of Christ?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being my strength even when I am weak. Help me not to rely on my own ability but to live in Your grace every day. Give me a heart that is focused, faithful, and patient, so that in good times and bad I follow You closely. Help me remember that You are always the faithful Lord, fully worthy of my trust. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will be strengthened in the grace of Christ and follow the Lord faithfully to the end.

t: God Will Surely Visit You
v: Joseph lived in Egypt, he, and his father’s house. Joseph lived one hundred ten years.
Joseph saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph’s knees.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”
Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.”
So Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.
b: Genesis does not end with Joseph’s achievements but with God’s promise. Joseph’s life was extraordinary: betrayed by his brothers, falsely accused and imprisoned, then raised by God to be prime minister of Egypt. Yet at the end of his life, what mattered most to him was not his position or glory but God’s faithfulness.

Near death, Joseph said twice, “God will surely visit you.” This was not a mere word of comfort; it was a declaration of faith from a lifetime of experiencing God. Looking back, there was God’s presence in every low point and God’s guidance in every crisis, so he firmly believed that God would lead his people in the future in the same way.

At that time Israel lived in Egypt, settled and prosperous, but Joseph knew Egypt was not the promised land. He charged his descendants to carry his bones with them when they left Egypt. This shows that his heart was always fixed on God’s promise, not on his present surroundings. True faith does not look only at what we have now; it trusts in what God will accomplish.

Our lives, too, have mountains and valleys, and sometimes we cannot see the road ahead. Joseph’s testimony reminds us that circumstances change and human ability is limited, but God’s promises never change. As God led us through yesterday, so he will keep watching over us tomorrow, because the faithful God never forgets his children.
a: Remember God’s grace
Count God’s past guidance to strengthen your faith today.
Fix your eyes on God’s promises
Don’t look only at present circumstances; look at God’s eternal plan.
Entrust the future to God
Believe that God will keep guiding and watching over your life.
q: When I face an uncertain future, do I believe God will surely watch over me?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being a faithful, covenant-keeping God. Just as You led Joseph all his life, You have never left me. When I face an uncertain future, give me faith to live not by sight but to believe Your promises. Help me fix my eyes on You, trusting that You will watch over me and guide me in Your way. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God will surely watch over me, and his promises never fail.

t: God So Loved the World, That Whoever Believes May Be Saved
v: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.
This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved the darkness rather than the light; for their works were evil.
For everyone who does evil hates the light, and doesn’t come to the light, lest his works would be exposed.
But he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be revealed, that they have been done in God.”
b: John 3:16 is called the heart of the whole Bible because it condenses the most precious truth of the gospel: God loves the world. The objects of God’s love are not a few especially good people but everyone. While people were still in sin and far from God, God had already reached out in love, giving his only Son, Jesus, to the world.

Jesus came into the world not to condemn people but to save them. Many assume God is always looking for our mistakes in order to rebuke and punish us, but God’s deepest desire is redemption. The cross is not God’s anger toward people; it is God’s love for them. Jesus bore the punishment of sin in our place, so that all who believe in him may have eternal life.

Yet God never forces anyone to accept his love. The passage says the light has come into the world, but some still choose darkness. Light exposes the truth and shines on what is hidden within us. So some would rather flee the light than face themselves. But those who are willing to come to the Lord, though they see their own weakness, also experience God’s forgiveness and renewal.

Today Jesus still extends his invitation to everyone. He does not ask us to become perfect before we come; he asks us to come as we truly are. When we are willing to receive his love and walk toward his light, our lives are changed and we gain an eternal hope.
a: Believe that God loves you
Don’t doubt your worth, for God has proven his love at the cross.
Come boldly into the light
Admit your weakness and need before God.
Live in the truth
Let God’s word guide your thoughts and your life.
q: Am I fleeing from God’s light, or am I willing to come to the Lord and be changed by him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for loving me so much that You gave Your only Son, Jesus, for me. Thank You that You did not come to condemn me but to save me. Help me come boldly into Your light, no longer hiding my weakness, but truly receiving Your forgiveness and renewal. May Your love fill my life, so that every day I live in Your truth and grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God loves me; I will walk in his light and live in his grace.

t: Faith in the Midst of Weakness
v: Gideon said to God, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken,

behold, I will put a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece only, and it is dry on all the ground, then I will know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken.”
It was so; for he rose up early on the next day, and pressed the fleece together, and wrung the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.

Gideon said to God, “Don’t let your anger be kindled against me, and I will speak but this once. Please let me make a trial just this once with the fleece. Let it now be dry only on the fleece, and on all the ground let there be dew.”
God did so that night; for it was dry on the fleece only, and there was dew on all the ground.
b: Gideon is a wonderfully real person in the Bible. When God called him to deliver Israel, he was not a hero brimming with confidence; he was full of doubt and unease. So he twice asked God for a sign, hoping to confirm that this was truly God’s will.

From a human point of view, Gideon seemed to lack faith, but God did not rebuke him. God knew Gideon’s weakness and understood his struggle. So God patiently answered his request, revealing his will through the miracle of the fleece twice. We see that God is not a harsh master but a Father who understands our weakness.

Yet Gideon’s story does not encourage us to demand a miraculous sign for everything. It shows us that God can lead a weak person into strength. The later Gideon no longer hid in a winepress threshing wheat; he led three hundred men to defeat the Midianite army. What changed him was not the dew on the fleece but learning, step by step, to trust God.

We are often like Gideon: anxious about an unknown future, afraid of God’s call, hesitant before challenges. But God does not give up on us because of our weakness. He delights to lead, support, and strengthen our faith, turning our reluctance into willingness to follow, and our fear of failure into brave obedience.
a: Be honest with God about your weakness
Don’t hide your fears and doubts.
Learn to trust God’s leading
God knows the road ahead better than we do.
Take one step in faith
Don’t stay waiting for confirmation; begin to obey God.
q: Is there something God has already stirred me to do, but I keep delaying out of fear?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for understanding my weakness and showing compassion for my limits. When I am afraid, hesitant, and lacking faith, support me and strengthen me. Help me not merely to seek confirmation, but to learn to trust and obey You. May I grow step by step in Your leading, as Gideon did, and live out the mission You have entrusted to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will trust God’s leading and step forward in faith, even in weakness.

t: Living a Spirit-Filled Life
v: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ, to God, even the Father;
b: Paul urges believers to live as wise people, not foolish ones. Wisdom is not an abundance of knowledge or a quick mind; it is knowing God’s will and living according to it. A truly wise person does not ask, “What do I want to do?” but, “What does the Lord want me to do?”

Paul especially speaks of “redeeming the time.” Our greatest asset in life is not money but time. Money lost can be earned again, but time once gone cannot return. So the wise cherish each day God gives, investing their lives in what has eternal value instead of wasting them on meaningless pursuits.

Paul then says, “Don’t be drunken with wine, … but be filled with the Spirit.” Drunkenness means being controlled by wine; being filled with the Spirit means being guided by God. Everyone is influenced and controlled by something: some by emotions, some by desires, some by circumstances. God’s will is that we be led by the Holy Spirit, so that we live out the life of Christ.

A Spirit-filled person shows three marks: a mouth full of praise, a heart full of joy, and a life full of thanksgiving in all things. Even when circumstances are not perfect, he finds peace and hope in God, because his focus is not on circumstances but on the Lord who rules over them.
a: Treasure the time God gives
Spend your time on what God considers important.
Seek the Holy Spirit’s guidance
Pray daily, and let God lead your thoughts and decisions.
Cultivate a thankful life
Learn to count God’s blessings each day.
q: What is controlling my life right now: circumstances, emotions, or the Holy Spirit?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving me precious life and time. Help me to be wise, to understand Your will, and to treasure each day You entrust to me. Fill me with the Holy Spirit and guide my thoughts, words, and actions, so that I live a life that pleases You. May my mouth always praise You, and my heart always give You thanks. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will be filled with the Holy Spirit and live a wise and thankful life.

t: Caring for One Another as One Body
v: For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.
For in one Spirit were we all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all made to drink into one Spirit.
For the body is not one member, but many.
But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.
The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.”
No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.
Those parts of the body, which we think to be less honorable, on these we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable parts have more abundant propriety;
whereas our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part,
that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another.
When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.
b: Paul uses the body to describe the church, helping us understand a key principle of God’s Kingdom: unity is not sameness but working together though different. A body has eyes, ears, hands, and feet, each with its own function, yet together they fulfill one mission. In the same way, God created each person differently and gave each different gifts and roles.

Many people fall into one of two traps: pride, thinking they are more important than others, or low self-worth, thinking they have no value. But Paul reminds us that the eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need for you,” nor can the hand despise itself for not being an eye. Every member God has placed has his good purpose; no one is superfluous.

Especially precious is that God gives greater honor to those members who seem weaker. In human eyes some are more visible and some are hidden; some stand in front, some work behind the scenes. But in God’s eyes every faithful person is equally precious. Those who pray quietly, serve unnoticed, and offer care and companionship are the very strength the church cannot do without.

So God wants us to learn to care for one another. When one suffers, all share the burden; when one is blessed, all rejoice. We are not rivals but family, joined by life. When everyone is willing to support and build up one another, the body of Christ grows in health and shows God’s glory.
a: Accept your role
Thank God for creating the unique you, and faithfully carry out his commission.
Honor every member
Appreciate others’ gifts, and also treasure your own worth.
Learn to care for one another
Reach out to those in need, sharing burdens and joys together.
q: Do I value every member God has placed in the body, and am I willing to walk in step with my brothers and sisters?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for placing me in the body of Christ as one of its members. Take away my pride and my low self-worth, and let me see the value of myself and of others in Your eyes. Help me learn to care for, support, and build up one another, so that we together, in one heart and mind, build Your church, for the glory of Your holy name. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will care for my brothers and sisters and build the body of Christ together with them.

t: Looking Up to the God Who Rules over All
v: “Can you bind the cluster of the Pleiades, or loosen Orion’s belt?
Can you lead out the constellations in their season? Or can you guide the Bear with her cubs?
Do you know the laws of the heavens? Can you establish the dominion of it on the earth?
“Can you lift up your voice to the clouds, that abundance of waters may cover you?
Can you send lightnings, that they may go? Do they report to you, ‘Here we are?’
Who has put wisdom in the inward parts? Or who has given understanding to the mind?
Who can number the clouds by wisdom? Or who can pour out the bottles of the sky, when the dust runs into a mass, and the clods of earth stick together?
“Can you hunt the prey for the lioness, or satisfy the appetite of the young lions,
Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God, and wander for lack of food?
b: When Job fell into terrible suffering, he kept bringing questions to God, hoping to understand why it had happened. But when God answered him, he did not directly explain the suffering; he led Job to look up at the whole universe. God asked, “Can you bind the cluster of the Pleiades? Can you guide the Bear with her cubs?” so that Job would see that humans are finite and God is infinite.

We often want answers to every question in life, but God wants us to know who he is. When we look only at our problems, they grow huge; when we see the God who created the heavens and rules the universe, the problems may remain, but they are no longer the center of our lives. Faith is not knowing all the answers; it is trusting the One who holds them.

God not only governs the vast starry sky; he also cares for life on earth. He provides prey for the lion and meets the needs of the raven’s young. If even the birds are in God’s care, how much more his beloved children! Often we think we have been forgotten, when in fact God has been watching over and providing for us all along.

In the end Job understood that life’s greatest peace is not fully understanding God but fully trusting him. When we admit our limits and turn our eyes from our problems to God, we can have a steady heart even in the storm. The Lord who governs the courses of the stars is also governing our lives.
a: Turn your eyes from the problem to God
Don’t think only about the difficulty; think about God’s greatness.
Believe in God’s care
Since God cares for all creatures, he will surely supply your needs.
Learn to trust God in the unknown
Even when you don’t understand, believe God still reigns.
q: When I meet something I can’t understand, am I demanding answers, or trusting the God who rules over everything?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being the Lord who created the heavens and the earth and rules over all things. When I face what I do not understand, help me see not only the problem but also Your greatness and faithfulness. Let me believe that You know my situation and will care for my needs. Give me a steady heart, able to trust You in every circumstance. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will look up to the God who rules over all, believing he will watch over my life.

t: When God Closes a Door
v: They went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus didn’t allow them.
Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.
A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him, and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.
b: Paul and his companions were eager to preach the gospel, but unexpectedly the Holy Spirit stopped them twice. First he did not let them go into Asia, and then he did not allow them into Bithynia. From a human point of view, what they were doing was good, the work of spreading the gospel, so why would God close the door?

This passage shows us that God’s will is not only that we do the right thing, but that we do what he wants, at the right time and in the right place. Often we think a blocked road is failure, when God may be steering us toward something better. When God closes a door, he is not rejecting us; he is preparing another door.

When Paul reached Troas, God made his will known through a vision. A man of Macedonia pleaded, “Come over and help us.” So the gospel entered Europe for the first time, opening a new chapter in mission. Had Paul clung to his own plan, he might have missed God’s greater leading. Obeying God’s guidance is often more important than our own plans.

Life also has many closed doors. Some plans cannot be realized, some roads lead nowhere, some opportunities suddenly vanish. But don’t lose heart, because God sees the future we cannot see. When one door closes, don’t keep staring at it; keep following the Lord and wait for him to open a new way.
a: Accept God’s hindrance
Sometimes God’s “no” is also God’s protection.
Keep an obedient heart
Don’t cling to your own plans; seek God’s guidance.
Believe God has a better plan
Even when the road is unclear for now, keep trusting the Lord.
q: Is there a door that has recently closed, through which God is guiding me toward a new direction?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when my plans are blocked and the road is not what I expected, help me not to complain or lose heart, but to learn to trust Your leading. Let me believe that Your ways are higher than my ways and Your thoughts higher than my thoughts. Give me a sensitive heart that can understand Your guidance, and the courage to obey Your will. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will trust God’s leading, believing that when he closes a door, he also opens a way.

t: Those Who Trust in God Will Not Be Put to Shame
v: The king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spoke and said to Daniel, “Your God whom you serve continually, he will deliver you.”
A stone was brought, and laid on the mouth of the den; and the king sealed it with his own signet, and with the signet of his lords; that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
Then the king went to his palace, and passed the night fasting: neither were instruments of music brought before him; and his sleep fled from him.
Then the king arose very early in the morning, and went in haste to the den of lions.

When he came near to the den to Daniel, he cried with a lamentable voice; the king spoke and said to Daniel, “Daniel, servant of the living God, is your God, whom you serve continually, able to deliver you from the lions?”
Then Daniel said to the king, “O king, live forever!
My God has sent his angel, and has shut the lions’ mouths, and they have not hurt me; because as before him innocence was found in me; and also before you, O king, have I done no hurt.”

Then was the king exceedingly glad, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no manner of hurt was found on him, because he believed in his God.
b: Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den not because he had done wrong but because he was faithful to God. He knew that continuing to pray might cost him his life, yet he kept worshiping God. True faith is not believing in God when things go well; it is choosing to follow him faithfully even in danger and under pressure.

When the stone sealed the mouth of the den, from a human view everything seemed finished. But what people saw was a sealed den; what God saw was the moment to rescue. God sent his angel to shut the lions’ mouths, so that the fierce lions could not harm Daniel. God’s power far exceeds human limits and the threat of circumstances.

The passage notes that no harm was found on Daniel because he trusted in his God. What protected Daniel was not luck or coincidence but his unwavering trust in God. Faith is not a guarantee of no storms; it is knowing that God reigns in the storm.

Life has its own “lions’ dens”: illness, pressure, misunderstanding, setbacks, or hardship. But Daniel’s story reminds us that when we faithfully trust God, God is with us. Even in a dark pit, do not lose hope, for God is still able to deliver.
a: Stay faithful under pressure
Don’t let circumstances change your trust in God.
Believe God rules over all
Human power is limited; God’s power is limitless.
Entrust difficulties to God
Even in the lions’ den, believe in God’s presence.
q: When I face the lions’ den of my own life, am I still willing to trust God steadfastly?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being the God who delivers. When I face difficulty, pressure, and challenge, give me a steadfast faith like Daniel’s. Help me not to retreat because of circumstances or lose heart because of hardship. Let me know that You still reign and Your power is greater than any crisis. Keep me, so that in every situation I follow You faithfully. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will trust God steadfastly, for he will keep me in times of trouble.

t: Receiving Comfort and Becoming a Comfort
v: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort;
who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
For as the sufferings of Christ abound to us, even so our comfort also abounds through Christ.
But if we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation. If we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which produces in you the patient enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer.
Our hope for you is steadfast, knowing that, since you are partakers of the sufferings, so also you are of the comfort.
b: Paul calls God “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort.” God is not only a distant ruler; he is a Father who knows our tears and understands our pain. When we experience loss, setbacks, illness, or hardship, God has not left us. He is right beside us, holding us up with his love.

Paul himself endured many afflictions, persecutions, and pains, yet he discovered something precious: every time he suffered, God’s comfort came too. God does not always remove every difficulty at once, but in the midst of it he gives strength, peace, and hope, so that we can keep going.

More wonderful still, God comforts us not only for our own sake. Paul says God comforts us so that we can comfort others. Having walked through the valley, we understand the hurting better; having experienced God’s support, we can bring hope to others. Often the scars in our lives become blessings for serving others.

So do not belittle the hardships you have been through. God can turn tears into testimony, wounds into blessing, and pain into strength to comfort others. When we share the grace we have received, we become an encouragement to others and let more people see God’s kindness and faithfulness.
a: Draw near to God in affliction
Believe God understands your pain and wants to comfort you.
Remember God’s grace
Recall how God led you through the valley in the past.
Become a comforter
Share the comfort you have received with those in need.
q: Am I willing to let the grace I have experienced become a blessing of comfort to others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for being the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. Thank You that You never left me in my affliction and weakness. Comfort my heart with Your love and presence, and make me a blessing to others, sharing the comfort I have received from You with those in need. May my life bear witness to Your grace and faithfulness. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will receive God’s comfort and become a vessel of comfort to others.

t: Living Under God’s Plumb Line
v: Thus the Lord Yahweh showed me: behold, he formed locusts in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and behold, it was the latter growth after the king’s mowings.
It happened that, when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, “Lord Yahweh, forgive, I beg you! How could Jacob stand? For he is small.”
Yahweh relented concerning this. “It shall not be,” said Yahweh.
Thus the Lord Yahweh showed me: behold, the Lord Yahweh called for judgment by fire; and it devoured the great deep, and would have devoured the land.
Then I said, “Lord Yahweh, cease, I beg you! How could Jacob stand? For he is small.”
Yahweh relented concerning this. “This also shall not be,” said the Lord Yahweh.
